messages.subject_clean: weighted means in stat_summary - how can I accomplish this?
messages.body_plain:
ggplot is able to use weights for barplots etc, but is it possible to
send weights to stat_summary functions? The default functions only
give me unweighted means/standard errors and despite many hours of
trying I havent been able to figure out how to send weights to
data.fun (I am not too cozy with R nor ggplot2 yet).

Can anyone show me the way?

This works for regular mean:

someData<-data.frame(variable=c("dog", "dog", "chicken", "chicken"),
value=c(5,4,4,5), weights=c(1,1,0.5,0.5))

testmean<-function(x){mean(x)}

p<-ggplot(someData, aes(x=variable, weight=weights))
p<-p + stat_summary(aes(x=variable, y=value), fun.y=testmean,
geom="point")
p

I am also using faceting with my original data, so just hardcoding the
weights vector will not help.

thank you in advance,
Indrek

messages.subject: Re: Using a background image
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Regarding this old subject, Paul Murrell announced (*) a new set of
functions to deal with raster graphics in R. Using the dev version of
R, one can now do this,

require(pixmap)

as.raster.pixmapRGB <- function(x) {
    nr <- nrow(x@red)
    r <- rgb((x@red), (x@green), (x@blue))
    dim(r) <- x@size
    r
}

 picture <- read.pnm(system.file("pictures/logo.ppm", package="pixmap")[1])

background = function(picture){
       function() rasterGrob(picture)

}

d = data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10)

p <- qplot(x,y,data=d) + theme_bw() +

       opts(panel.background = background(picture))

I imagine it will be possible to use these new and exciting tools to:

- create filling patterns (e.g. for bw histograms)
- make general filling gradients
- combine the advantages of vector and raster graphics for large
images (the axes and text could be vector, whilst the many tiles could
be converted to raster for better rendering and huge improvement in
file size).

(*) http://developer.r-project.org/Raster/raster-RFC.html

Best,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: fill pattern of barchart as "coarse hatching pattern".
messages.subject_clean: fill pattern of barchart as "coarse hatching pattern".
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

There was a discussion on this subject here some time ago, I think the
conclusion was that since Grid graphics do not provide filling
patterns for polygons it is currently not possible to do this in
ggplot2. However, you might like to hear of the very recent addition
of grid.raster() to the development version of R (*), which might help
in filling barplots with more freedom in the future. A basic example
adapted from Paul Murrell's follows,

library(grid)
# create a pattern
x11(width=4, height=4)
grid.grill(h = seq(0, 1, length=50), v = seq(0, 1, length=50),
vp=viewport(angle=45))
# capture it as a bitmap
hatch <- grid.cap()
dev.off()

# now draw the barplot
year <- c(1993, 1996, 1998, 2001)
minpop <- c(20, 50, 50, 115)
maxpop <- c(50, 240, 240, 150)

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(plotViewport(),
             viewport(xscale=c(1991, 2003), yscale=c(0, 250)))
grid.xaxis(at=year)
grid.yaxis()
grid.rect()
# white bars
grid.rect(x=unit(year, "native"), y=0,
          width=unit(1, "native"), height=unit(maxpop, "native"),
          just="bottom", gp=gpar(fill="white"))
for (i in 1:length(year)) {
    grid.clip(x=unit(year[i], "native"), y=0,
              width=unit(1, "native"), height=unit(maxpop[i], "native"),
              just="bottom")
    # pattern fill
    grid.raster(hatch, width=1.5, height=1.5)
}
grid.clip()
# redo bar borders
grid.rect(x=unit(year, "native"), y=0,
          width=unit(1, "native"), height=unit(maxpop, "native"),
          just="bottom", gp=gpar(fill=NA))
popViewport(2)
grid.clip()

With enough motivation it might just be possible to hack a geom for
ggplot2 that uses this grid.clip() trick.

(*) : http://developer.r-project.org/Raster/raster-RFC.html where this
example was taken.

Best,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: how to best deal with overplotting
messages.subject_clean: how to best deal with overplotting
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

I don't see how marginal histograms help you with overplotting - they
do not tell you anything about the joint distribution.  The technique
that I'd try first is bin2d facetted by your classification variable.
Otherwise, you could do something like:

ggplot(mydf, aes(x, y)) +
 geom_point(data = transform(mydf, catvar = NULL), colour = "grey80") +
 geom_point(aes(colour = catvar)) +
 facet_wrap(~ catvar)

to get a facetted scatterplot plot with all points in the background
of each plot.

Hadley

messages.subject: plotting POSIXct timestamps on the x-axis fails around the 2009 DST date on WinXP
messages.subject_clean: plotting POSIXct timestamps on the x-axis fails around the 2009 DST date on WinXP
messages.body_plain:
Hey folks,

I'm seeing some strangeness when I try to plot a time series using
ggplot2 in R 2.9.2 on WinXP.  Basically, when the last date in the
range is near the daylight savings day (November 1st here in the US),
I get an "Error in seq.int <http://seq.int>(0, to - from, by) : 'to' must be finite".
Scale_x_datetime doesn't seem to help things.

The daylight savings date thing may or may not be related - all I know
is if the last timestamp in the series I'm trying to plot is between
2009-10-31 03:00:00 PDT and 2009-11-01 00:00:00 PDT, this error
appears, and the DST transition occurs at 2009-11-01 02:00:00 PDT.

I can't reproduce this error around the 2008-11-02 DST transition, and
this behavior does not manifest on Mac OS 10.6.

Anyone have any thoughts as to what might be going on?

cheers,
Tarek.

tester <- function (n, timestep = 3600, origin = "2009-10-30"){
  dy <- data.frame(time = as.POSIXct(seq(0, (n-1) * timestep,
timestep), origin=origin), value = rnorm(n))
  qplot(time, value, data=dy)
}

tester(27) # works
tester(28) # fails with "Error in seq.int <http://seq.int>(0, to - from, by) : 'to'
must be finite"
# 28:49 fail with "Error in seq.int <http://seq.int>(0, to - from, by) : 'to' must be
finite"
tester(49) # fails with "Error in seq.int <http://seq.int>(0, to - from, by) : 'to'
must be finite"
tester(50) # works

Some updates to the http://yeroon.net/ggplot2 web application:

- SYNTAX MODE: webapp now includes a super secret tiny arrow in the
center-bottom of the page, that opens a syntax window. This is a
feature some people requested. It should interactively show you the
code used to plot the current graph. Please let me know your
experiences, and if it generates sensible code.

- Now works in IE: there was some bug that prevented the application
from properly displaying in Internet Explorer. It should be fixed now.
Supported browsers are Internet Explorer 6+, FireFox 1.5+ (PC, Mac),
Safari 3+, and Chrome, however a recent browser is more than highly
recommended. For best performance use Chrome 3 or Safari 4.

Furthermore, many people seem to have problems uploading their data.
To avoid any confusion: if the filename ends with .csv, the data is
imported using read.csv("filename.csv",header=T); if it ends
with .sav, it uses read.spss("filename.sav"), and in all other cases
it uses read.table("filename.txt", header=T). I'm working on something
better. Any suggestions on this part are welcome too.

Jeroen

messages.subject: Radar plot with polar coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I did a field experiment, and measured some fruit variables:
- length
- width
- weight
- pulp weight
- ...

I would like to plot each fruit by means of an 'ideogram', meaning as
a radar plot, where the score for each variable is plotted on an axis.
I thought the coord_polar()-function would be appropriate for this,
since in this way, it is possible to visualise different 'types' of
fruits by different radar forms.

I transformed my dataset to this form (originally, each fruit was one
record):

Fruit	Variable	   Score
1	Length	   22
1	Width	   16
1	Weight	   135
1	Pulp weight  56
...

Subsequently, I used following code:

F<-read.table("fruit.txt",header=T)

P<-ggplot(F,aes(Score,Variable))+geom_point()  # conventional point
plot #
P + coord_polar ()  # each variable is represented by one axis, and
scores are indicated by points #

I would like to connect the different scores for one fruit to
facilitate the interpretation of the figure and to distinguish
different fruit 'types'.
If I use the command:

P + coord_polar() + geom_line()

The lines on the polar plot are not straight (due to coordinate
conversion), but I would like straight lines.
Of course, I could use the 'stars' package, but I want to classify the
fruits on harvest location and/or season of harvesting.

Does anybody know how to produce straight lines between the different
scores in the polar plot?

Thanks!
Sebastiaan

messages.subject: Re: Altering Legend
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, Nov 20, 2009 at 17:54, AC Del Re <acd...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I believe
> the problem I'm encountering is related to the 'size' option in the
> geom_point function, as the legend size is quite large ( large symbols
> in the legend key for one of the groups plotted) when using this
> option and resumes normalcy if omitted (see attachment). Also, how might I
> remove one
> of the legends entirely, if desired (e.g., wt.del).

Please do not repost the same questions several times and provide
reproducible code in your email. You code is good except that we do
not have the data to test it. If you cannot provide a data sample,
make a fake one, e.g. :

    grief2 <- data.frame(n.sess=runif(10), del=runif(10),
risk=as.integer(runif(10)*3), wt.del=runif(10))

Now I cleaned your code a bit and here is what I got to:

library("ggplot2")

ggplot(grief2, aes(x=n.sess, y=del, shape=factor(risk), size=wt.del))
+ geom_point() +
    scale_area(to = c(4,10)) +
    scale_shape(solid = FALSE, name="Risk Level", labels = c("normal",
"at-risk", "chronic"))

The remarks are:
- you don't need both scale_size and scale_area, scale_area is a
particular case of scale_size
- you don't need breaks for a variable that is already a factor: the
breaks are the level of the factor

Using this, I do not get you strange artifact on the "Risk level"
legend that you have. Which version of ggplot/R are you using?
You can remove the legend entirely with opts(legend.position = "none")
but I don't think you can remove one of them. But you would not want
to do this: you mapped the size (the area actually) to one of your
variables so you want to explain that in the legend, otherwise your
reader would not know why the symbols have different sizes and what
that relates to.

JiHO
---

messages.subject: Re: fill pattern of barchart as "coarse hatching pattern".
messages.subject_clean: fill pattern of barchart as "coarse hatching pattern".
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

A small update on the Grid aspect: I played a little with the idea of
tiling a raster motif and clipping it to a rectangle. The idea is as
follows: 1) create a motif and rasterize it with grid.cap; 2) make the
drawDetails method of the new grob to calculate how many repeats of
the motif are needed for a particular outline size; 3) clip the tiled
motif to the rectangular outline. This setup ensures that the user is
in control of the size of the motif and that this size is maintained
for different rectangle sizes (also works with dynamic resizing).

The code below works with R devel, though I ran into some weird
device-dependent problems (posted to R-dev). The working output is
attached.

Best,

baptiste

library(grid)

dots <- function(..., width=0.5, height=0.5){
  x11(width=width, height=height)
  grid.points(x=unit(0.5, "npc"), y=unit(0.5, "npc"), ...)
  m <- grid.cap()
  dev.off()
  invisible(m)
}
.dots <- dots()
 grid.raster(.dots)

plus <- function(..., width=0.5, height=0.5){
  x11(width=width, height=height)
  grid.points(x=unit(0.5, "npc"), y=unit(0.5, "npc"), pch="+",
gp=gpar(cex=3), ...)
  m <- grid.cap()
  dev.off()
  invisible(m)
}
.plus <- plus()
 grid.raster(.plus)

slash45 <- function(..., width=0.5, height=0.5){
  x11(width=width, height=height)
  grid.segments(...)
  m <- grid.cap()
  dev.off()
  invisible(m)
}
.slash45 <- slash45()
 grid.raster(.slash45)

bslash45 <- function(..., width=0.5, height=0.5){
  x11(width=width, height=height)
  grid.segments(0, 1, 1, 0, ...)
  m <- grid.cap()
  dev.off()
  invisible(m)
}
.bslash45 <- bslash45()
 grid.raster(.bslash45)

grid45 <- function(..., width=0.5, height=0.5){
  x11(width=width, height=height)
  grid.polygon(...)
  m <- grid.cap()
  dev.off()
  invisible(m)
}

.grid45 <- grid45()

## grid.raster(.grid45)

tile.motif <- function(m, nx=10, ny=nx){
  cols <- matrix(rep(m, nx), ncol=ncol(m)*nx, byrow=F)
  matrix(rep(t(cols), ny), nrow=nrow(cols)*ny, byrow=T)
}

## quartz()
## grid.raster(tile.motif(.dots, 2, 3))
## grid.raster(tile.motif(.grid45, 2, 3))
## grid.raster(tile.motif(.slash45, 2, 3))
## grid.raster(tile.motif(.bslash45, 2, 3))

patternGrob <- function(x=unit(0.5, "npc"), y=unit(0.5, "npc"),
                        width=unit(1, "npc"), height=unit(1, "npc"),
                        motif=matrix("white"), AR=1,
                        motif.width=unit(5, "mm"),
                        motif.height=AR*motif.width,
                        pattern.offset=c(0, 0), # unimplemented
                        default.units="npc",
                        clip=TRUE, gp=gpar(fill=NA), ...)
  {
    grob(x=x, y=y, width=width, height=height,
         motif=motif, motif.width=motif.width,
         motif.height=motif.height, clip=clip, gp=gp, ..., cl="pattern")
  }

widthDetails.pattern <- function(x) x$width
heightDetails.pattern <- function(x) x$height

drawDetails.pattern <- function(x, recording=TRUE){

##   calculate the number of tiles
  nx <- ceiling(convertUnit(x$width, "in", value=TRUE) /
                convertUnit(x$motif.width, "in", value=TRUE)) + 1
  ny <- ceiling(convertUnit(x$height, "in", axisFrom = "y", value=TRUE) /
                convertUnit(x$motif.height, "in", axisFrom = "y",
value=TRUE)) + 1

  width <- convertUnit(x$width, "in")
  height <- convertUnit(x$height, "in", axisFrom = "y")

##   clip the raster
  pushViewport(viewport(x=x$x, y=x$y,
          width=x$width, height=x$height, clip=x$clip))

  grid.raster(tile.motif(x$motif, nx, ny), width=nx*x$motif.width,
                         height=ny*x$motif.height)
  upViewport()

##   overlay the rectangle
  grid.rect(x=x$x, y=x$y,
          width=x$width, height=x$height,
          just="center", gp=x$gp)
}

g1 <- patternGrob(x=0.2, y=0.1, width=unit(0.2, "npc"),
                  height=unit(0.1, "npc"),
                  clip=TRUE, motif=.dots)

g2 <- patternGrob(x=0.7, width=unit(3.7, "cm"),
                  height=unit(5.2, "cm"),
                  clip=TRUE, motif=.grid45)

g3 <- patternGrob(x=0.2, width=unit(0.2, "npc"),
                  height=unit(2.3, "cm"),
                  clip=TRUE, motif=.slash45)

g4 <- patternGrob(x=0.7, y=0.1, width=unit(2, "in"),
                  gp=gpar(fill=NA, col="blue", lwd=2),
                  height=unit(0.1, "npc"), AR=3,
                  clip=TRUE, motif=.bslash45)

g5 <- patternGrob(x=0.5, y=0.8, width=unit(1, "npc"),
                  gp=gpar(fill=NA, col="blue", lwd=2),
                  height=unit(0.1, "npc"),
                  clip=TRUE, motif=.plus)

quartz()
grid.newpage()
lapply(ls(pattern="g[[:digit:]]"), function(g) grid.draw(get(g)))

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Dec 1, 2009 at 11:17 PM, hadley wickham <h.wi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> Of course the next problem is coming up with a nice library of textures...
>>
>> That would be the nice part...
>> You'd think that must have been studied already somewhere (base
>> graphics' histograms maybe?, or xfig <
>> http://www.xfig.org/userman/fig-format.html >). For a quick try it
>> would just be a case of importing bitmap graphics (EBImage) and saving
>> the raster textures. Eventually one would like to be able to generate
>> textures on-the-fly should the need arise (resolution problems, etc.).
>
> You would think so, but in my experience there has been little work
> done on coming up with aesthetically pleasing and perceptual
> distinctive shapes or line types or textures.

page 317, table 10.2 of Wilkinson's Grammar of graphics presents an
overview of textures. They might differ in i) granularity (spacing
between marks), ii) pattern (dots or lines, etc), iii) orientation
(tilt of the lines).

>From this table, I have the impression that:

1- for filling patterns as for linetypes and point shapes there is
only a limited choice of variants, and only a few of them can ever be
distinguished in a given plot.

2- considering 1- and the lack of literature regarding which patterns
are good or bad (visual artifacts and ease to distinguish), I think
one should settle for a small set (maybe 5 to 7 max) of widely used
patterns. To me this is the same problem as for the default linetypes
and point shapes in base R: they remain dictated by publication
habits, until a real cognitive study can be found.

Another question that may arise is what should happen when two objects
overlap? Should the two patterns mix or remain in opaque layers?

Best,

baptiste

> Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would use tikz for this (I see it has also been suggested while I'm
writing this),

require(ggplot2)
require(RColorBrewer)

d <- data.frame(x=1:2, y=1:2, f=c("women", "men"))

ggsave("simpleEx.pdf",
 qplot(x, y, data=d, colour=f) +
   scale_colour_brewer(palette="Set1"))

## find the RGB colours
a <- sapply(brewer.pal(3,"Set1"),col2rgb)
round(a / 255, 3)

and then, in your tex file,

\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{tikz}

\begin{document}

% a <- sapply(brewer.pal(3,"Set1"),col2rgb)
% round(a / 255, 3)
%      #E41A1C #377EB8 #4DAF4A
% [1,]   0.894   0.216   0.302
% [2,]   0.102   0.494   0.686
% [3,]   0.110   0.722   0.290

\definecolor{women}{rgb}{0.894,0.102,0.110}
\definecolor{men}{rgb}{0.216,0.494,0.722}

\begin{figure}
\centering\includegraphics{simpleEx}
\caption{Men (\protect\tikz{\protect \fill[men] (1ex,1ex) circle
    (1mm);}), Women (\protect\tikz{\protect \fill[women] (1ex,1ex)
circle (1mm);}).}
\end{figure}

\end{document}

I might be possible to automate this a little with e.g. Sweave.
Another option might be to generate the little colour dots with R and
include them as inline graphics,

pdf("dot1.pdf", width=2.54/20, height=2.54/20)
grid.points(0.5,0.5,pch=19,gp=gpar(col=cols[1]),default.units="npc")
dev.off()

pdf("dot2.pdf", width=2.54/20, height=2.54/20)
grid.points(0.5,0.5,pch=19,gp=gpar(col=cols[2]),default.units="npc")
dev.off()

\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{tikz}

\begin{document}

\begin{figure}
\centering\includegraphics{simpleEx}
\caption{Women (\protect\includegraphics{dot2}), Men
(\protect\includegraphics{dot1}).}
\end{figure}

\end{document}

Best,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Dear list members

I'm working on a problem where I wish to use a hexbin display, but the
colour for each hexagon should not be the density or the count, but a
summary of a third variable.

Here's a simple and dumb example. In Hexland, there are several types of
people living, type A to E. The various types of people prefer to live
in different areas of Hexland; e.g., type A people prefer living near
the centre, type B some distance from the centre, &c.

I wish to summarise this with five plots/facets, where each plot shows a
hexagonal display of Hexland, but where the colour of each hexagon is
determined by the proportion of people of the chosen type (facet) that
lives there. For instance, for the first facet, type A, the colour
should be dark near the middle and lighter far away, and the colour
scale should show a percentage, from 0 to 100 % (e.g., white to black).

To do this, I guess I have to create a modified stat_hexbin, but I'm not
at all sure how to do this, and there is not much documentation on it
either. Also, a complicating factor may be that the colour of a hexagon
should be determined based on the number of people of the chosen type in
the hexagon *and* the total number of people in that hexagon, i.e.,
across all facets (so that for a specific hexagon, the 'sum' of the
(greyscale) colours across all facets would be black).

If this is too difficult, a plot not using facetting, and just showing
the proportion of a specified type for each hexagon would be OK. (I
could then use a loop to obtain five similar plots, in essence showing
the same data).

Any ideas how to accomplish this? Of course, any suggestions on other
nice graphical displays for these type of data would also be very welcome.

Here are some simple example data:

library(ggplot2)
n=10000
k=5
x=runif(n)-.5
y=runif(n)-.5
types=LETTERS[1:k]

dist=sqrt((x^2+y^2)/.5)

f=function(x) {
    p=rep(1,k)
    p[round(1+x*(k-1))]=5
    sample(types,1,prob=p)
}
people=sapply(dist,f)

dat=data.frame(x,y,people=factor(people,levels=types))

# Plots showing the data
qplot(x,y,data=dat,colour=people)

qplot(x,y,data=dat,geom="hex")

messages.subject: Re: order aesthetic with geom_area
messages.body_plain:
This is a pretty frequently asked question, did you search the list
archives?

add in this

d$value <- factor(d$value, levels=c("whale", "kitten", "panda"))

the order that the vector for levels is given will be the order used
(you don't need ordered=T).

If you need that to be dynamic (ie according to counts or something),
then I think you'll need to calculate that yourself.

I wonder if adding an optional (and over-riding) "group-level-order"
variable to aes might help document this? I know it's the "wrong"
place (the data frame is the "right" place to declare this info), but
clearly this is something that confuses people.

--J

messages.subject: Re: order aesthetic with geom_area
messages.body_plain:
James,
Yes, I've tried exactly that, and several variations thereupon. But if
you run this code, you'll see that while the factors get resorted in
the legend, and the colors are shuffled, their respective bands get
stacked in the same order.

d <- melt(data.frame(week = sequence(52), "panda","kitten","whale"), c
("week"))[-2]
d$eaten<-rpois(52*3, 2) #because using the poisson distribution makes
it Science.

p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(x=week, y=eaten, group=value)) + geom_area(aes
(fill=value))

d$value <- factor(d$value, levels=c("whale", "kitten", "panda"))

p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(x=week, y=eaten, group=value)) + geom_area(aes
(fill=value))

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(2,1)))
vplayout<-function(x,y)
    viewport(layout.pos.row=x,layout.pos.col=y)
print(p1,vp=vplayout(1,1))
print(p2,vp=vplayout(2,1))

messages.subject: Re: order aesthetic with geom_area
messages.body_plain:
There's two issues at stake here:

 * the order in which the labels appear on the legend, controlled by the scale

 * the order in which the areas are stacked, controlled by the order
in which the values appear in the data, and putatively the order
aesthetic.  However, there are a few bugs which I'm still working on.
 See http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/labels/data#issue/33 and
http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/labels/data#issue/34

Regards,

Hadley

Hi,
Yes, If I am understanding correctly what you want to do it should be
possible

hexTapply that should give you something close. I am working on an
update

take a couple of more weeks.
If you need more help let me know.

Nicholas

On Fri, 04 Dec 2009 11:31 -0600, "hadley wickham" <h.wi...@gmail.com>

> How tied to hexagons are you?  It's pretty easy to do with square
> bins, with ddply.  Otherwise, you'll need to look at the hexbin
> package and see if it's possible to use a custom aggregation function
> for each cell.  Once you have that I can tell you how to display it
> with geom_hex.
>

> ideas.

> Hadley

> On Fri, Dec 4, 2009 at 11:19 AM, Karl Ove Hufthammer
> <Karl.Hu...@math.uib.no> wrote:
> > Dear list members
> >
> > I'm working on a problem where I wish to use a hexbin display, but the
> > colour for each hexagon should not be the density or the count, but a
> > summary of a third variable.
> >
> > Here's a simple and dumb example. In Hexland, there are several types of
> > people living, type A to E. The various types of people prefer to live
> > in different areas of Hexland; e.g., type A people prefer living near
> > the centre, type B some distance from the centre, &c.
> >
> > I wish to summarise this with five plots/facets, where each plot shows a
> > hexagonal display of Hexland, but where the colour of each hexagon is
> > determined by the proportion of people of the chosen type (facet) that
> > lives there. For instance, for the first facet, type A, the colour
> > should be dark near the middle and lighter far away, and the colour
> > scale should show a percentage, from 0 to 100 % (e.g., white to black).
> >
> > To do this, I guess I have to create a modified stat_hexbin, but I'm not
> > at all sure how to do this, and there is not much documentation on it
> > either. Also, a complicating factor may be that the colour of a hexagon
> > should be determined based on the number of people of the chosen type in
> > the hexagon *and* the total number of people in that hexagon, i.e.,
> > across all facets (so that for a specific hexagon, the 'sum' of the
> > (greyscale) colours across all facets would be black).
> >
> > If this is too difficult, a plot not using facetting, and just showing
> > the proportion of a specified type for each hexagon would be OK. (I
> > could then use a loop to obtain five similar plots, in essence showing
> > the same data).
> >
> > Any ideas how to accomplish this? Of course, any suggestions on other
> > nice graphical displays for these type of data would also be very welcome.
> >
> > Here are some simple example data:
> >
> > library(ggplot2)
> > n=10000
> > k=5
> > x=runif(n)-.5
> > y=runif(n)-.5
> > types=LETTERS[1:k]
> >
> > dist=sqrt((x^2+y^2)/.5)
> >
> > f=function(x) {
> >    p=rep(1,k)
> >    p[round(1+x*(k-1))]=5
> >    sample(types,1,prob=p)
> > }
> > people=sapply(dist,f)
> >
> > dat=data.frame(x,y,people=factor(people,levels=types))
> >
> > # Plots showing the data
> > qplot(x,y,data=dat,colour=people)
> >
> > qplot(x,y,data=dat,geom="hex")

while facet_grid has no problem. Please see the attached plots, and
the code below. I am using ggplot2 version 0.8.3.

0.55, 0.55, 0.65, 0.65, 0.65), type = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L,
1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), .Label = c("a", "b", "c"
), class = "factor"), permumin = c(1, 3.3982873053574, 2.49509155245557,
1, 3.08529057823006, 2.09998223949833, 1, 0.477121254719662,
1.66673732299373, 2, 0.477121254719662, 1.22337408302429), permumax = c(1,
3.39967372148104, 2.553763005257, 2, 3.39234515536120, 2.19730989144648,
6, 3.33505651943909, 1.81688992821307, 14, 2.83473851890384,
1.40337585404783)), .Names = c("rho", "type", "permumin", "permumax"
), row.names = c(19L, 20L, 23L, 25L, 26L, 29L, 31L, 32L, 35L,
37L, 38L, 41L), class = "data.frame")

messages.subject: Re: Latex caption suggestions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

tikzDevice is excellent indeed and works perfectly (as far as I could
see) with ggplot2 but I'm not sure how it helps for Hadley's question.
Since the caption probably shouldn't be part of the figure itself, I
think the (newly updated) pgfSweave package from the same authors
would be more useful here. What would be needed is a way to extract
the different legend items from a ggplot, so one could do the
following,

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \begin{center}

<<fig=TRUE, device="tikz">>=
library(ggplot2)

p = qplot(...)
print(p)
@

    \caption{Men (\Sexpr{getFirstItemofLegend(p)}), Women
(\Sexpr{getSecondItemofLegend(p)})}
  \end{center}
\end{figure}

I don't know if \Sexpr{} could deal with tikz code though.

Best,

baptiste

messages.subject: geom_text question
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am interested in better understanding how to insert text (and additional data) into a plot. For example,

x<-rnorm(1:20)
y<-x+rnorm(1:20)
plot(x,y)
xrng<-range(x)
yrng<-range(y)
data1<-qplot(x,y)
caption<-paste(strwrap("Adj.means:  first= .111  second= .222
 third= .333",15),collapse="\n")                    #this setup seems messy
data1+geom_text(aes(x,y,label=caption),
 data=data.frame(x=xrng[2],y=yrng[1]),
 hjust=2,vjust=-2,size=3)

How can I get the text to be lined up and uniform?

#like this
Adj. means:
 first =      .111
 second = .222
 third =     .333

Also, is there an easy way to enter in tables of data (such as the beta coefficients from lm(y~x)) but in a way where the coefficient names are included and where the line breaks can be specified to my liking?

reg<-lm(y~x)
beta1<-reg$coefficients[1:2]
caption<-paste(strwrap(beta1,collapse="\n")
data1+geom_text(aes(x,y,label=caption),
 data=data.frame(x=xrng[2],y=yrng[1]),
 hjust=2,vjust=-2,size=3)

Finally, is there additional documentation on geom_text? I have read Hadley's book and perused the ggplot2 website and am interested in learning more.

Thank you,

AC

messages.subject: Re: geom_text question
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I wrote a basic geom_table that one can use with annotate to add a
table at a specific location in a ggplot. The table is typically drawn
from a data.frame but it may contain only a single row/column. I
defined some specific lists of settings for the appearance,
unfortunately these themes appear quite redundant with ggplot2's own
theming system because ggplot2 does not define theme elements for the
geoms.

library(ggplot2)
library(ggExtra) # http://code.google.com/p/ggextra/

x<-rnorm(1:20)
y<-x+rnorm(1:20)

xrng<-range(x)
yrng<-range(y)

p <- qplot(x,y)
caption <- as.data.frame(strwrap("Adj.means:  first= .111  second=
.222  third= .333",15))

p + annotate("table", table=caption, x=1, y=-2, theme=theme.list()) + theme_bw()

reg<-lm(y~x)
beta1<-reg$coefficients[1:2]

caption <- as.data.frame(round(beta1,3))
p + annotate("table", table=caption, x=1, y=-2,
           theme=theme.list(show.rownames=T, show.colnames=T),
cols=expression(beta[1]))

HTH,

baptiste

On Wed, Nov 25, 2009 at 03:41, Paulo Eduardo Cardoso
<pauloed...@gmail.com> wrote:
> This is something to think about. I don't know how ggplot2 manage to
> plot cartesian coordinates or what is happening when we set a coord_map
> ().
>
> We'd need to know how ggplot2 deals generally with the relation
> between plot region/aspect ratio.

I must admit I was never sure of what exactly coord_map() was doing.
What's sure is that the aspect ratio should indeed no change when the
size of the plotting window changes (which it currently does). I
think/hope this is what Hadley is referring to when he talks about
"integrating the functionality of coord_equal to coord_map". This
would allow for further testing of this potentially very cool
functionality.

I have been plotting quite a few lat/lon based maps, in particular
within a GIS class (so we had directly comparisons). The method that I
found to be most reliable was to use:
    coord_equal(ratio=cos(mean(latitude)*pi/180))
this works with latitude in decimal degrees, on small enough maps, far
enough from the poles. So of course, it is not a complete solution.

The other method is of course to transform all distances to meters and
plot that together with
    coord_equal(ratio=1)
which is the default, so
    coord_equal()
is enough. The conversion to meters can be done through projections
inside some geostatistics packages in R (gstat, geoR) or, if you want
to keep things a bit simpler, using a function that takes lat and lon
as input directly. I have found rdist.earth in fields not to be very
precise and have coded one from several sources I found online. It is
attached here. I can guarantee that the results are accurate but,
since it currently uses a loop, it can also be very slow. The way I
use it is:
    data$x = geod.dist(refLon, refLat, data$lon, refLat)
    data$y = geod.dist(refLon, refLat, refLon, data$lat)
I hope this helps a bit, for now.

Oh and, by the way Hadley, while coord_equal() works it also has the
annoying effect of forcing the plot to be square. The fact that I want
to coordinates to be equal does not mean that the region I want to
plot cannot be a rectangle. I gave you a few illustrated examples with
the behaviour I would expect a while back (email thread "ggplot2,
coord_equal and aspect ratio" started on Fri, Jan 11, 2008 by
jo.ir...@gmail.com), but in case they got lost, look at page 5 of
this file:
    http://jo.irisson.com/teaching/villefranche/mapping_and_interpolation.pdf
I would rather have the x axis go from about 7.295 to 7.34, so that I
can easily juxtapose  plots such as on page 6 for example. Currently
much of space is taken by useless grid squares that contain no data.

Thanks in advance for your help,

JiHO

messages.subject: Re: fill pattern of barchart as "coarse hatching pattern".
messages.subject_clean: fill pattern of barchart as "coarse hatching pattern".
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

grid.raster is indeed a raster format and won't scale like a vector
format when you zoom in. It is possible to make a vector filling
pattern for rectangles in R, but to me it makes more sense to use this
new raster function. Unlike data and text, I see no gain in having a
scale-independent output for patterns, quite the contrary in fact.

1- If you use a raster output format, it won't make any difference anyway.

2- If you edit the pdf with, e.g. Illustrator, the pattern is one
single object with a clipping attribute, not a group of many small
points/lines. It seems more suited to the task.

3- The file size would be much smaller than a fully vector output, and
it's presumably faster.

4- grid.raster is not like grid.rect: it can perform interpolation
between points, so you see a smoother output when zooming in. Granted
it's not sharp and scale-independent, but does it need to be?

5- No weird artifacts from pdf viewers.

6- as you mention, gradients and exotic textures can be used as well
as more classical tiling patterns.

In addition, I have the impression that such patterns are almost
intrinsically of absolute size. For instance, If I make an histogram
and I want the filling pattern to be little squares, I will need to
specify a sensible density for the pattern to be visible inside the
rectangles. If the  motif has a given size (e.g. 5mm) it makes sense
to me to give it a good but finite resolution because it is designed
to be viewed at a given size. If I need to produce a very large
graphic for a poster or something, I would use a different motif size,
and then choose the resolution accordingly.

I guess it would be interesting to make a small example with both
techniques and gauge the respective advantages/drawbacks.

Best,

baptiste

While all points are valid and I mostly agree with them, this one is
critical to me:

> 4- grid.raster is not like grid.rect: it can perform interpolation
> between points, so you see a smoother output when zooming in. Granted
> it's not sharp and scale-independent, but does it need to be?

a raster line will never look and more importantly print as sharply as
a vector line. So printing a rectangle filled with a raster pattern of
slanted lines for example will result in a sharp black boundary and
greyish inside lines. I am probably a bit anal about that but, to me,
it really make an important difference. To submit the plot the a paper
I would probably recreate the patterns in Inkscape a posteriori for
the sake of having it all vector (even if the print guys are often not
very good at their jobs, they tend to screw up vector plots less than
raster ones, in my little experience).

> In addition, I have the impression that such patterns are almost
> intrinsically of absolute size. For instance, If I make an histogram
> and I want the filling pattern to be little squares, I will need to
> specify a sensible density for the pattern to be visible inside the
> rectangles. If the  motif has a given size (e.g. 5mm) it makes sense
> to me to give it a good but finite resolution because it is designed
> to be viewed at a given size. If I need to produce a very large
> graphic for a poster or something, I would use a different motif size,
> and then choose the resolution accordingly.

I would tend to suggest the contrary. Let say I have a bar chart with
such patterns which are spaced so that they look good for a 7x10cm
publication graph (probably a 1 pt line every ~1.5, 2 mm). If I want
to print this plot on a poster at size 20x30 cm I probably do not want
a thin line every 2mm. I more likely to need a 1.5mm line every 5-8
mm. So basically I want to take the PDF of my plot and scale it up,
including the pattern. For this, raster patterns would be
inappropriate.

JiHO

d <- volcano

cols <- grey(t(d)/max(c(d)))
xy <- expand.grid(x=seq(0, 1, length=ncol(d)), y=seq(0, 1, length=nrow(d)))

rect2raster <- function(g){

 with(g, rasterGrob(matrix(gp$fill, ncol=length(unique(x))), mean(x),mean(y)))
}

g1 <- rectGrob(xy$y, rev(xy$x), 1/(nrow(d)), 1/(ncol(d)),
              gp=gpar(col=NA, fill=cols))

g2 <- rect2raster(g1)

system.time({
pdf("comparison-rect.pdf", width=10, height=10/2*ncol(d)/nrow(d))
replicate(10, grid.draw(g1))
dev.off()
})

pdf("comparison-raster.pdf", width=10, height=10/2*ncol(d)/nrow(d))

})

messages.body_plain:
I played a bit more with the vector pattern, one can now specify
points or lines. My main concern now is that "grid.vpattern" is not
vectorized(*) like grid.rect or grid.points, etc. Of course one can
remedy this with Vectorize but I'm a bit worried about the efficiency.
Do you know other examples of grid functions that are not vectorized?

(*) the other kind of vector if you follow me!

## example below, try resizing the window

library(grid)

source("http://gridextra.googlecode.com/svn/trunk/R/vpattern.r")

grid.newpage()
grid.vpattern(width=unit(3,"cm"), height=unit(0.5,"npc"),
              motif="points", motif.params=list(pch=2,
gp=gpar(cex=0.5)), clip=T)

grid.newpage()
grid.vpattern(width=unit(0.3,"npc"), height=unit(0.5,"npc"),
              motif="segments", motif.params=list(angle=45))

grid.newpage()
grid.vpattern(width=unit(3,"cm"), height=unit(5,"cm"),
              motif="segments", motif.params=list(angle=-45))

Cheers,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have a variable with values c(0, 1, 2) which I'm using to color the
points of my plot. They're probably best represented as an ordered
factor, but I would like to use a continuous color scale, so I'm using

from the legend, but I can't figure out how. Is this possible?
Alternatively, is there some way to use a continuous scale with
something that is not a numeric variable?

Thanks!

-Joe

messages.subject: Hexbin plot in grey scale
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I need to do a hexbin plot in greyscale for publication. It works fine
in color (working example below), but when I add scale_fill_grey() to
it, it generates an error message. In Googling about on this I found
http://learnr.files.wordpress.com/2009/08/latbook.pdf, which
duplicates Lattice examples in ggplot2, but the hexbin plots from
Lattice are in grey but the author leaves the ggplot2 plots in color.
That makes me wonder if it's possible to do them in grey.

Any ideas?

Thanks,
Bob

# Generate some data:
pretest2   <- round( rnorm( n=5000, mean=80, sd=5) )
posttest2  <- round( pretest2 + rnorm( n=5000, mean=3, sd=3) )
pretest2[pretest2>100] <- 100
posttest2[posttest2>100] <- 100
temp=data.frame(pretest2,posttest2)

# This works fine, but is in color:
ggplot(temp, aes(pretest2, posttest2))  +
  geom_hex( bins=30 )

# Adding scale_fill_grey() yields,
# "Error: Continuous variable () supplied to discrete scale_grey."
ggplot(temp, aes(pretest2, posttest2))  +
  geom_hex( bins=30 ) + scale_fill_grey()

Hi Joe,

You can set the breaks in the scale to be whatever you want. So for instance:

df0 <- data.frame(variable=rep(0:2, c(30,30,30)), x=rnorm(90), y=rnorm(90) )
p <- ggplot(df0, aes(x,y, fill=variable))
p + geom_point() + scale_colour_continuous(breaks=c(0,1,2))

HTH
david

messages.subject: Re: Invisible linetypes in in pdf
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

if you do send a bug report you might want to make it clear that it's
not related to ggplot2 by providing a raw Grid example,

x = seq(0, 10, length=10000)
y = cos(x)

pdf("test-pdf.pdf", width=4, height=4)
pushViewport(viewport(xscale=c(0, 10), yscale=c(0, 6)))
for(ind in 1:5)
grid.lines(x, y+ind, gp=gpar(lty=ind), default.units="native")
dev.off()

quartz(type="pdf", file="test-quartz.pdf", width=4, height=4)
pushViewport(viewport(xscale=c(0, 10), yscale=c(0, 6)))
for(ind in 1:5)
grid.lines(x, y+ind, gp=gpar(lty=ind), default.units="native")
dev.off()

The algorithm that computes the dashed lines is clearly working better
for pdf than for quartz when the points are very dense.

I can't reproduce the disappearance of the lines in the pdf device
though, I'm wondering if it's not a ggplot2 bug?

Best,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Invisible linetypes in in pdf
messages.body_plain:
Regarding the original bug (invisible lines for pdf), does anyone know
if it has been reported to the R team?

I think I nailed the problem to an unfortunate side-effect of lineend="butt",

pdf("test.pdf")
grid.newpage()
grid.lines(gp=gpar(lty="13"))
grid.newpage()
grid.lines(gp=gpar(lty="13", lineend = "butt"))
dev.off()

Illustrator recognises a line in both pages in the pdf output, however
in the second page the line pattern has zero solid length because of
the lineend.

It may be that this is the correct behavior and that quartz() actually
cheats, I don't know. From the perspective of ggplot2, it might good
to change the lineend parameter in geom_path ?

Best,

baptiste

messages.subject: ggplot2 0.8.4
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I've just uploaded the latest version of ggplot2 to cran and so it
should be available on your local mirror in the next couple of days.
It's basically just a big set of bug fixes, but there are a couple of
new features.  I've included a complete changelog below.

I'll be working on ggplot2 quite a bit over Christmas, so please let
me know if you've discovered a new bug - the list of all bugs I
currently know about is available
http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues, and if you look closely
you'll notice I've been working a lot of ggplot2 0.8.5 which includes
another big round of bug fixes.  I'm hoping to release this in the
next week or two, and then begin on a big layout rewrite which will
herald ggplot2 0.9.

Regards,

Hadley

ggplot2 0.8.4 (2009-12-08) ----------------------------------------

* aes and aes_string both convert prefixes to full names
* aesthetics: corrected list of aesthetics to include american spelling of
  colour as well as base R abbreviations
* aesthetics: fix bug in detecting which aesthetics are calculated
* aes_string treats NULL as "NULL"
* annotate now works with missing x and y (e.g. for geom_rect)
* continuous scale limits now automatically sorted
* coord_polar: fix bug if breaks not all inside limits
* facet_wrap: can now specify both ncol and nrow without getting an error
* facet_wrap: now works with statistics that produce both x and y values (e.g.
  stat_qq)
* fullseq now adds additional break on bottom if necessary, so that the
  include.lowest argument in cut never comes into play (this the source of a
  potential bug in histograms)
* geom_boxplot: alpha now affects fill colour of boxes only
* geom_path correctly switches to segments if varying alpha used (thanks to
  Karl Ove Hufthammer for the report and Baptiste Auguie for the fix)
* geom_point: the alpha aesthetic now also affects the fill.
* geom_ribbon always sorts input to avoid problems with certain pathological
  inputs
* geom_smooth was incorrectly applying alpha to line colour in the legend
* nullGrob renamed to zeroGrob to avoid name conflict with grid
* position_collide now works with missing values
* position_stack: fixed bug in detection of overlap for negative values
* scale_discrete_position now uses drop argument to force dropping of unused
  levels
* scale_gradient, scale_gradient2 and scale_gradientn now uses label
  parameters, if supplied
* scale_x_inverse, scale_y_inverse now actually work, and added recip as alias
* stat_qq now correctly groups results
* stat_smooth will not try and fit a line to 2 or fewer points (previously
  didn't try for only 1 point)
* stat_spoke now works with reversed scales
* grouping: now consistent between different geoms (Issue #33)

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

   I am a new ggplot2 user and I have hit a wall with something that
in principle should be relatively easy to do. I would like to generate
a scatter plot using a color coded gradient for the data, over which I
would like to overlay a single point, at coordinates x=0.002652,
y=0.054668, in a different color (say red) to highlight it from the
rest of the set. Here is the code I am currently using which is only
generating the first plot. A working example of how to solve this
challenge would be most appreciated. Thanks so much for your help!

 ------- code:

library(ggplot2)
pTable <- read.csv("test.csv", header=T)
attach(pTable)
png(filename="test.png" ,width=800, height=600)
p <- qplot(sigma, R,
            colour = Z,
            data = pTable,
            xlab = "sigma",
            ylab = "Y",
            main = "Title")
p + scale_colour_gradientn(colour = topo.colors(10))
p + geom_point(0.002652,0.054668,colour = "red", size = 3)
dev.off()

The best way would be to put the point coordinates in an own data.frame

I would do it like this:

point <- data.frame(disp=300,wt=4)
ggplot(mtcars,aes(disp,wt,colour=gear)) + geom_point() +
    scale_colour_gradientn(colour = topo.colors(10)) +
    geom_point(data=point,size=3,colour="red")

 Stefan

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 0.8.4
messages.body_plain:
Here's what I have on my list, in no particular order:

should have subtitle
think about double axes
legend alignment within box
key table with rows and columns
legend shouldn't overlap with plot
legend.position != "right"
should be able to override label alignment in legends
finally do facet label wrapping correctly
should be able to set fixed size for any element (incl. panel) - and
should be able to compute for ggsave
secondary axis which is a function of the primary axis
don't clip axis labels
aspect ratio and axis labels
should be able to control apperance of strips: T = always display, F =
never display, and NA = display if > 1
figure out how to do margins and padding properly
axis line should be plotted on top of panel.background
device size
should support multiple pages
margins should have bigger gaps
make sure facet labels span across all columns
make entire strip function a theme setting
more flexible strip formating to look like labels
some way of plotting nested factors with varying levels so that they
line up nicely - wrap within grid

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 0.8.4
messages.body_plain:
Great! (and good luck :-) )

If I'm not mistaken most of these features are implemented in lattice,
it might give you some inspiration. lattice is also faster at
arranging the plot elements on the page (pushing a viewport, then
drawing), although I prefer the way it's done with ggplot2 (assigning
viewports to the grobs).

One thing that I didn't see in the list is the ability to specify,

- manual axis breaks, limits and labels for each panel, with more
control than scales="free" (lattice gives the option of using a list
to override the defaults)

- manual spacing between panels.

Also a general wish: for most elements of a plot, I really like
lattice's functional and object oriented approach: you have a default
function that returns a graphical object (say, a facet strip), but you
can replace it with your own function to create a very original plot
(e.g. use the strip space to draw a sparkline).
The same remark applies to axes: I remember a recent request on this
list to draw chemical structures as axis labels. One could imagine a
user-defined function that returns an axis with custom grobs for the
labels. Of course one would have to ensure that all these elements
have a well defined size so that the layout knows how much space needs
to be allocated.

All the best,

baptiste

messages.subject: Scale training with non-mapped data
messages.body_plain:
I ran into, what seemed to me, an odd inconsistency in how scales are trained.  I was trying to force the y-axis to go down to zero, so I thought I'd use geom_point to add a single point with a y value of 0.  (I know about scale_y_continuous(limits) and coord_cartesian(ylim); I'll explain later why these options would not work in my situation.)

library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(data=mtcars, aes(x=cyl, y=hp)) + geom_point()
p #scales go from 4-8 on x-axis, 50-~350 on y-axis

# want to force y-axis to go down to zero
p + geom_point(x=4, y=0, colour="red")
# identical to p

p + geom_point(data=data.frame(cyl=4, hp=0), colour="red")
# y axis now goes to 0

p + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y), data=data.frame(x=4,y=0), colour="red")
# same as when aes mapping was to cyl and hp

A geom_point with a non-mapped x and y did not affect the training of the y-axis; the same values mapped to a data.frame did.  Now, the documentation I read (PDF of draft of the book) talked about the scales being trained from the datasets, and didn't mention any fixed values being part of it.  I can even see where the fixed values should not be part of training (say, on a graph with a mapped colour aesthetic, but annotated text in black, black should not be part of the color scale), but it surprised me at first.  Is this how training is supposed to work?

The problem I was trying to solve was closer to

p + facet_grid(gear~., scale="free")

where I wanted each of the y-axes to go down to 0, but the scaling and maximum to be based on the facet.  I could get the effect I wanted with

p + geom_point(aes(x=x,y=y,gear=gear),
  data=data.frame(x=c(4,4,4), y=c(0,0,0), gear=c(3,4,5)), colour="red") +
  facet_grid(gear~., scale="free")

(I am using a red dot in these examples so that it shows up, I actually used colour=NA). Is there a better way to do this?

If not, as a feature request, would it be possible to only partially specify either scale_y_continuous(limits) or coord_cartesian(ylim)? That is, so that a syntax like

p + facet_grid(gear~., scale="free") + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA))

would work?  The lower limit is fixed, but the upper limit is based on the data.  limits=c(NA,50) would also be acceptable for specifying only the upper limit, for example.  limits=c(NA,NA) would be the same as limits not being specified at all.  My proposed use case is for faceted free scales that should at least have a common base, which may be outside the range of the data.

--
Brian Diggs, Ph.D.
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery, Oregon Health & Science University

that I can (eventually) find ways to speed up the drawing.

Yes, because that's not really a layout issue - it's a scaling issue.

that you could do would be to come up with some suggestions for what
the syntax might look like.

> - manual spacing between panels.

This is tricky, but I'll definitely be thinking about it.

> Also a general wish: for most elements of a plot, I really like
> lattice's functional and object oriented approach: you have a default
> function that returns a graphical object (say, a facet strip), but you
> can replace it with your own function to create a very original plot
> (e.g. use the strip space to draw a sparkline).

Using functions for this is fine, the problem is figuring out just
what the arguments of each function should be.  It's definitely
reasonable to pass the strip function the title of the strip, but if
you want to do something more interesting you need to pass in the data

> labels. Of course one would have to ensure that all these elements
> have a well defined size so that the layout knows how much space needs

I'll definitely think about this, but I'm not sure number of times it
would be used justifies the amount of work involved.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,

I just looked in to this myself, and decided that when you set values
they can't be automatically added to the scale mapping - otherwise (as
you mention) things like geom_point(colour = "red") wouldn't work.
The approach that you are using to force inclusion of the values is
the one that I'd suggest, but instead of using geom_point with colour
= NA, use geom_blank, which is specifically designed for this type of
situation. Maybe all you really need is a thin wrapper around
geom_blank that makes it easy to force inclusion of certain values:

expand_limits <- function(...) {
  data <- data.frame(...)

  geom_blank(aes_all(names(data)), data, inherit.aes = FALSE)
}

p + expand_limits(x = 0)
p + expand_limits(x = c(1, 9))
p + expand_limits(x = 0, y = 0)

It will work with any aesthetic.

What do you think?   I'll probably include this in ggplot2 0.8.5.

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Hadley,

Thanks for the response and ideas.

I had not noticed geom_blank before, but that is clearly the better choice than geom_point with colour=NA.  Also, I had not seen the inherit.aes option before, and could not find any documentation about it.  I assume that if it is true, then that layer does not inherit any of the mappings from the mapping specified in the ggplot() call.  That is very handy for this sort of adjustment.  Where would I find documentation on this (and any other such gems)?

I also had not seen aes_all before (I learned a lot from just a few lines of your code).  When I went to read about that function more, I found out that none of aes, aes_string, nor aes_all have entries in the list of functions that you get from help(package=ggplot2) (nor on the HTML help via help.start() -> Packages -> ggplot2) although there are help pages for them directly (help(aes) does work).

Your expand_limits function works well.  I tried various permutations, including expanding scales other than the axes and it worked.  For example:

p + geom_point(aes(colour=factor(gear))) + expand_limits(colour="other")
# adding another level to the discrete colour scale

p + geom_point(aes(colour=gear)) + expand_limits(y=0, colour=8)
# extending the continuous colour scale

p + facet_grid(gear~.) + expand_limits(gear=6)
# adding to gear adds another facet

p + facet_grid(gear~., scale="free") + expand_limits(gear=6, y=0)
# must set a y value for this one, otherwise there is a facet with no data on which to free scale

Testing edge cases:

p + expand_limits()
# works, effectively, p

p + expand_limits(x=c(0,10), y=0)
# works, length of arguments must be the same length or 1.

p + geom_point(aes(colour=factor(gear))) + expand_limits(x=c(0,10), y=0, colour="other")
# works
p + geom_point(aes(colour=factor(gear))) + expand_limits(x=c(0,10), y=0, colour=c("other","other2"))
# works
p + geom_point(aes(colour=factor(gear))) + expand_limits(x=c(0,10), y=0, colour=c("other","other2","other3"))
#Error in data.frame(...) :
#  arguments imply differing number of rows: 2, 1, 3
p + geom_point(aes(colour=factor(gear))) + expand_limits(x=c(0,10), y=0) + expand_limits(colour=c("other","other2","other3"))
# works

p + facet_grid(gear~., scale="free") + expand_limits(gear=6) + expand_limits(y=0)
#Error in if (length(range) == 1 || diff(range) == 0) { :
#  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
# fails for same reason that the following fails
p + facet_grid(gear~., scale="free") + expand_limits(gear=6)
#Error in if (length(range) == 1 || diff(range) == 0) { :
#  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

So while you can have multiple expand_limits, it is not necessarily true that expand_limits(...) + expand_limits(...) will give the same result as expand_limits(...,...) and sometimes one will work where the other won't.

I look forward to seeing this in 0.8.5.

--
Brian Diggs, Ph.D.
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery, Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: qqplot where x and y have different length?
messages.subject_clean: qqplot where x and y have different length?
messages.body_plain:
Hello ggploters !

I would like to plot the distribution of a parameter of interest and
the distribution of a subsample of this parameter in a quantile-
quantile-plot. It is in the nature of things the the subsample is a
shorter vector as the total population. I would like to know if I can
use ggplot for this purpose?
Since the data for ggplot has to be stored in a data frame I have no
idea how to plot a qqplot. Using the R base graphics it is quite easy
because I can use vectors of different length as x and y values, e.g.:

> nrow(population_dataset)
[1] 50000
> nrow(subsample_dataset)
[1] 5000
> qqplot(x=population_dataset$parameter1, y=subsample_dataset$parameter1) # works fine

Can I do the same with ggplot? Is it possible in ggplot to use
variables of two different datasets as x and y values???

Thanks for any help

TIM

messages.subject: bug: legend.position
messages.body_plain:
I have a legend with very long labels, so I thought it would look
better on the bottom or top of the plot, but I find that
legend.position in opts doesn't seem to work (tried on ggplot2 0.8.3
and 0.8.4). Simple reproducible example:

the_data = data.frame(
	x = c( 1 , 2 )
	, y = c( 1 , 2 )
	, z = c( 'a' , 'b' )
)

p = ggplot(
	data = the_data
	, mapping = aes(
		x = x
		, y = y
		, colour = z
	)
)+
geom_point()

#works
print(p)

#same, works
print( p + opts(legend.position = 'right') )

#all fail
print( p + opts(legend.position = 'left') )
print( p + opts(legend.position = 'bottom') )
print( p + opts(legend.position = 'top') )

#works, but plots the legend on top of the plot
print( p + opts(legend.position = c(.5,1), legend.justification='top') )

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology
Dalhousie University

Looking to arrange a meeting? Check my public calendar:
http://tr.im/mikes_public_calendar

~ Certainty is folly... I think. ~

messages.subject_clean: Order of boxes in faceted boxplots
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot2 users,

I am new to this group and I would first like to thank Hadley for this
wonderful package!

My question is related to faceted boxplots and I have attached sample
code to illustrate the problem I have:

Example 1)
## Ordering works fine
tier1 <- letters[1:10]
tier2 <- c(rep("tier-a",5), rep("tier-b",5))
values <- runif(10, 1, 10)
d <- data.frame(tier1, tier2, values)
gg <- ggplot(d)
gg + geom_bar(aes(x=reorder(tier1, values), y=values)) + facet_wrap
(~tier2, scales="free")

Example 2)
## Ordering does not work
tier1 <- c("d", "b", "e", "a", "f", "f", "a", "b", "g", "e")
tier2 <- c(rep("tier-a",5), rep("tier-b",5))
values <- runif(10, 1, 10)
d <- data.frame(tier1, tier2, values)
gg <- ggplot(d)
gg + geom_bar(aes(x=reorder(tier1, values), y=values)) + facet_wrap
(~tier2, scales="free")

In example one the ordering of boxes in the boxplot works absolutely
perfect. However, in the second example the ordering does not work. I
assume it has something to do with repeating values in vector "tier1".
Does anyone know how to circumvent this problem. I am not sure whether
this might be a bug in ggplot.

Many thanks for your help!

Best,

David

I don't think this is something ggplot can do.  See, for example:

http://learnr.wordpress.com/2009/07/02/ggplot2-version-of-figures-in-lattice-multivariate-data-visualization-with-r-part-4/#_figure_4_7

In particular, look at

gg + geom_bar(aes(x=reorder(tier1, values), y=values)) + facet_wrap

(~tier2)

using your second example.  Here, the empty levels of the factor are
not suppressed, and you see the facets have the x-axis categories in
the same order.  In fact, it is the same order as the levels in

with(d, reorder(tier1, values))

which suggests that the ordering takes place before the data is split
for faceting.  Also note that by default reorder sorts by the average
of all the values in the level.

--Brian Diggs

messages.subject: Re: ddply and multiple functions
messages.body_plain:
I suspect Hadley would prefer you to ask plyr questions on its mailing
list (which I'm cc'ing, for the historical record):
http://groups.google.com/group/manipulatr

On Dec 12, 9:56 pm, Felipe <mazatlanmex...@yahoo.com> wrote:
> Hi:
> ddply is able to apply two functions here...
> ddply(baseball, .(lg), c("nrow", "ncol"))
>
> but I get an error message when trying to apply mean and sd...
> ddply(baseball, .(year), c("mean", "sd"))

Right, because nrow() and ncol() are meaningful when applied to
dataframes, but what's the mean() or sd() of a dataframe? Makes no
sense! Remember what ddply does, it creates a bunch of little
dataframes by splitting on the specified column, so whatever functions
you ask ddply to perform have to be operations on a dataframe.

>
> It can be done with the following code but was wondering if it could
> be done with ddply.
> sd.avg<-ddply(baseball, c("lg", "year"), function(df)
> return(c(avg=mean(df$rbi), sd=sd(df$rbi))))
> sd.avg

Yep, that's what I'd do. (The "return" is superfluous, incidentally.
Functions in R always return the value of the last statement.) That
*is* being done with ddply.

 -Harlan

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, that's helpful.

In the meantime, I figured that I should not have this vertical line
after all, but that gives me another problem: the density of the data
is quite coarse along the y axis, therefore setting the y limit gives
me a very approximate end for the path. I found a ugly hack around it
but I guess there is a better way...

Consider this new data,

x <- seq(0, 2, length=1e3)
d <- data.frame(x=x, y=1/((x-1)^2 + 0.001) )

d$y[d$x < 1] <-  d$x[d$x < 1] -1

p <- qplot(x, y, data=d, geom="path")

# this gives me the same output as base graphics
p + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-10, 80))+
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-10, 80, by=10))

# here the path stops *before* the y limit
p + ylim(-10, 80)

# dummy hack to split the data by regions, just above the limit

d$group <- cumsum(abs(diff(c(0, d$y > 85))))

p %+% d + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-10, 80))+ aes(group=group)+
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-10, 80, by=10))

Thanks again,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Dec 14, 2009 at 22:57, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
> This is done already in 0.8.5 which I'll be realising either today or
> later this week. If you can't wait, see
> http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/tree/ggplot-0.8.5.

Great!

> (I've switched to using branches for releases, which I'm hoping will
> make certain things simpler in the long run)

So from what I see, development is still linear, meaning that the
master stopped and then all changes went to the 0.8.5 branch. So what
I should do if I want the bleeding edge is follow the new branch each
time (0.8.5, 0.8.6, 0.9 etc.) rather than the master.
I am afraid I don't really see the purpose of this new setup but I
guess there is one ;) I would just suggest that if you are trying to
reproduce svn-like release branches, that allow to:
1. only include some changes from the master into the release and
2. continue improving the release branch for point-releases after the
initial release is made
I would rather suggest a workflow such as:
        - work on master
        - tag 0.8.4 (the old way)
        - branch 0.8.5 *immediately*
        - work on master, change 1
        - work on master, change 2
        - work on master, change 3
        - switch to branch 0.8.5
        - merge changes 1 and 3 from master, 2 is not suited for this
release. This is not actually a merge operation but something like a
series of cherry-picking. You can use the method described in answer 2
of this stack overflow question:
         http://stackoverflow.com/questions/449541/how-do-you-merge-selective-files-with-git-merge
        to avoid doing all the cherry picking by hand.
        - tag 0.8.5 release on the 0.8.5 branch
        - checkout master
        - branch 0.8.6
        - work on master
        - checkout 0.8.5
        - fix a thing
        - tag 0.8.5.1
        - checkout master
        - work on master
        ...
This way, all development stays on master and other parties can just
follow that. Making a release is picking out the pieces you want from
the master and storing them in the release branch.

JiHO

I have some data which diverges at three locations. I want to cut the
y scale to a sensible value, but when I do that ggplot2 truncates the
data to the nearest points that fit within the plot window. Because of
the fast divergence of the data, there are only few points along the y
axis near the divergences, so the cut is done at very approximate
ordinates. This gives an unpleasant feeling that the data stops at
random y values.

The other solution that you proposed (coord_cartesian) connects
artificially the points on both sides of the divergence, which isn't
realistic for my data (there is a discontinuity).

A real life example is attached with the three versions. I finally
obtained the output I wanted (last version), but the code is really a
dirty hack. Basically I add a create a factor to split the data in
different regions, depending whether they are within or outside the
plot region. I then use this as a group argument in ggplot2 so that
lines in different groups are not connected.

Is there a better way to get the third output?

Best,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Dec 15, 2009 at 3:39 PM, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
>> The other solution that you proposed (coord_cartesian) connects
>> artificially the points on both sides of the divergence, which isn't
>> realistic for my data (there is a discontinuity).
>
> I'd say that's a bug in coord_cartesian.  Would you have some time to
> create a minimal example that shows that behaviour?  Then I can add it
> to my to do list.

I don't think this is a bug, more likely a new feature on my wishlist.
In fact my problem was a bit ill-posed yesterday.

Below is a minimal example that illustrates three possible behaviors
when a path is cut by the plot area. I was asking for the last one,
but I had overlooked an indetermination in the discontinuous path: is
it discontinuous on the left side, or the right side, or both?
Extending this procedure to curves that have several discontinuities
might be a bit trickier.

x <- seq(0, 1, length=100)
y <- ifelse( x-0.5 < 0 , -1, 1/abs(x-0.5))

d <- data.frame(x=x, y=y)

## the full scale plot shows a continuous path
p <-
ggplot(d, aes(x, y))+
  geom_path()

## restricting the y limit to 150
## this time the path is not continuous

p + ylim(-2, 150)
##  ... but the line actually stops at

inside <- d$y[d$y < 150]
inside[which.min(abs(inside - 150))]
## 66

## we can use coord_cartesian to set the limit

p + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-2, 150))

## now the line extends to the limit
## but the path is connected on the left again

## one workaround: split the path in different groups
## so that the points are not connected on one side of the divergence

discontinuous <- function(d, limit=150, side=c("right")){
  d$group <- 1
  first.outside <- min(d$y[d$y >= limit])
  breakpoint <- which(d$y == first.outside)
  breakpoint <- breakpoint + if(side == "right") -1 else 0
  d$group[seq(1, breakpoint)] <- 0
  d
}

d <- discontinuous(d)

p %+% d + aes(group=group) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-2, 150))

Cheers,

Baptiste

>
> Hadley

> http://had.co.nz/

ggplot(df,aes(x=x,y=y,colour=condition)) + stat_quantile()

Does anyone know how to fix that?

Thanks,

Simon Barthelmé

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Dec 17, 2009 at 01:21, Paulo Eduardo Cardoso
<pauloed...@gmail.com> wrote:
> ggplot() +
> geom_bar(data=Data,aes(x=factor(H),y=V),stat="identity") + facet_grid
> (A~.,scales="free_y") +
> geom_rect(aes(NULL, NULL, xmin = inicio, xmax = fim, fill = P), ymin =
> 0, ymax = max(Data$V),data = DT) +
> scale_fill_manual(values =alpha(c("blue","red"), 0.2))
>
> Error: Casting formula contains variables not found in molten data: A

facet_grid needs to have data to facet on and since facetting is
global, the data should be in the ggplot() call.

ggplot(Data) +
geom_bar(data=Data,aes(x=factor(H),y=V),stat="identity") +
facet_grid(A~.,scales="free_y") +

geom_rect(aes(NULL, NULL, xmin = inicio, xmax = fim, fill = P), ymin =
0, ymax = max(Data$V),data = DT) +
scale_fill_manual(values =alpha(c("blue","red"), 0.2))

should work.

JiHO

messages.subject: ggplot2 0.8.5
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm very pleased to announce ggplot2 version 0.8.5 - you can think of
it as an early Christmas present ;)

Hadley

New features

* geom_text gains parse argument which makes it possible to display
  expressions. (Implements #50)

* all scales now have legend parameter, which defaults to TRUE. Setting to
  false will prevent that scale from contributing to the legend (Implements
  #27)

* default axis labels and legend titles are now stored in the options, instead
  of in each scale. This fixes a long standing bug where it was not easy to
  set the label for computed variable, such as the y axis on a histogram.
  Additionally, it means default scales are only added to the plot until just
  prior to plotting, instead of the previous behaviour where scales where
  added as layers were added - this could cause problems if you later modified
  the underlying data. (Implements #28)

* coord_equal: when ratio = NULL (the default), it will adjust the aspect
  ratio of the plot, rather than trying to extend the shortest axis.

* x and y positions can be set to Inf or -Inf to refer to the top/right and
  bottom/left extents of the panel. (Implements #18)

* expand_limits(): a new function to make it easy to force the inclusion of
  any set of values in the limits of any aesthetic.

New features (minor)

* aesthetics: when _setting_ an aesthetic, you may only set it to a single
  value.  This was always a good idea, but now it is enforced with an
  informative error message.
* stat_contour bump up default number of contours
* stat_density2d: make number of grid points used for density estimation
  user controllable (implements #9)
* geom_bin now allows you to set whether bins used intervals of the form
  (a, b] or [a, b) with the "right" parameter (implements #20)
* geom_path: linejoin, lineend and linemitre are now user controllable
  (implements #24)
* scales: all scales check that breaks are supplied if labels are, and
  that breaks and labels are the same length (implements #40)
* scales: if breaks are a named vector, the names will be used as labels
  (thanks to suggestion by David Kahle)
* scale_colour_gradient, scale_colour_gradient2 & scale_colour_gradientn now
  have formatter argument to match scale_continuous
* updated citation to refer to the ggplot2 book

Bug fixes

* coord_cartesian now correctly sets limits when one or both of the position
  scales are non-linear.  (fixes #17)
* coord_equal: now works with non-linear scales (fixes #13)
* coord_map sets aspect ratio correctly (fixes #4)
* coord_polar correctly combines labels on end of axis if expressions
  (fixes #39)
* coord_trans now respects scale expand parameter (expansion occurs after
  transformation) (fixes #14)
* facet_grid with scales = "free" and space = "free" now calculates space
  correctly if the range of the scale is < 1 (fixes #1)
* facet_grid works once more when facetting with multiple variables in one
  direction (fixes #11)
* facet_wrap now sets aspect ratio correctly
* facet_wrap now maintains original order of data
* geom_hline and geom_vline now work with coord_flip (fixes #30)
* geom_path drops missing values at start and end of each line (fixes #41)
* scale_shape_discrete, scale_size_continuous, scale_alpha and
  scale_linetype_discrete added to scales to match naming convention of all
  other scales (fixes #47)
* legends now correctly calculate label widths (fixes #38)
* legends will only merge if both the title and all labels are the same.
  (fixes #16)
* legends: fix for bug #19: Legend with three constraints doesn't work
* stat_contour & stat_density2d: fix grouping bugs (issue #7)
* xlim, ylim: fix bug when setting limits of discrete scales

--

messages.subject: Graph Recommendations
messages.body_plain:
Wow, the new version of ggplot2 is great, Hadley! Thanks for making the legend parameters more flexible. I have altered the graph (discussed in a previous post) where I wanted one of the 2 legends removed.

I have a question for the group (and my apologies in advance if this is an inappropriate question for this group): Attached is the graph I have been working on and I am very interested in any feedback on it. I am really interested in expert opinion about how well the graph conveys important information and any aesthetic recommendations. Thank you, AC.

Description of graph:

Background.  Previous meta-analyses have concluded that grief counseling is effective only for patients experiencing complicated grief—i.e., extreme or chronic grief reactions that do not abate as normally expected over time.  In this analysis we demonstrate that the larger effect sizes for chronic grievers as compared with normal grievers are an artifact of differences in the length of treatment (number of sessions).  Poor outcomes for a third group, so-called at-risk grievers, do appear to be significantly lower than those for normal and chronic grievers.

Findings of univariate moderator analyses.  As was the case in previous reviews, we found a significant difference in effect size (D+) by treatment population, where superior outcomes were seen in studies involving chronic grievers.  In Figure 1 (below), the inset boxplot on the right illustrates this pattern of means, with the mean effect size (represented by a ‘+’ symbol) for the chronic group hovering at around 1.0, that for the normal group closer to 0.5, and even lower mean effects for the at-risk group.  (It also shows that the mean for the chronic group is quite a bit higher than the median, indicating that the large effect size for this group is strongly influenced by three studies reporting abnormally large effect sizes.)

Confounds among moderators.  However, the inset boxplot on the left in Figure 1 shows that client type (normal, at-risk, or chronic) was confounded with another significant moderator variable:  number of sessions, or treatment dosage.  In fact, the pattern of means for number of sessions mimics quite closely the pattern of means for effect size in the other inset boxplot, suggesting that the superior effect sizes for the chronic group might simply reflect the greater treatment dosage received by this group.

The main graph in Figure 1 illustrates how this confounding operates.  Effect size is plotted on the y axis as a function of number of sessions on the x axis.  Type of grief is represented by the shape of the point, with circles, triangles, and squares representing normal, at-risk, and chronic grievers, respectively.  The size of the point reflects the weight of the study in the meta-analysis (mostly a function of sample size, with larger points corresponding to studies with larger Ns, which therefore provide a more precise estimate of the population effect size).

Note the upward trend on this graph, reflecting the importance of number of sessions as a predictor of effect size.  As expected, studies with longer treatment durations tend to show greater effectiveness.  Note too that interventions tended to be longer in studies involving chronic grievers, with no study involving an intervention with fewer than 12 sessions, whereas many of the effect sizes for normal and at-risk grievers were derived from studies of interventions involving 10 or fewer sessions.

This figure shows that the straightforward interpretation of the differences in risk group means (inset boxplot on the right) may be misleading.  The superior effect size for chronic grievers may reflect the longer treatments in studies involving this population, rather than a greater responsiveness to treatment in this group.  To draw clear conclusions about this, it is necessary to study dosage and risk group simultaneously as predictors of effect size.  As we demonstrate subseauently in our multivariate moderator analyses, the apparent difference in effectiveness between normal and chronic grievers disappears completely when treatment duration is controlled, leading to very different conclusions about the importance of risk group, and very different implications about who can and cannot benefit from grief counseling.

messages.subject: Separate binwidths for faceted histogram
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would like to change the binwidth in a faceted histogram.

Here is an example of:
## I create some data
a <- data.frame(val=rnorm(1000, 0, 10), label="a")
b <- data.frame(val=rgamma(1000, 1, 20), label="b")
dat <- rbind(a,b)

# The v graph looks nice...
v <- ggplot(dat=dat, aes(x=val, y=..ncount..)) + geom_histogram() +
facet_grid(.~ label, scales="free")
print(v)

## ... but when I am trying to change the binwidth, the graph looks ugly.
u <- ggplot(dat=dat, aes(x=val, y=..ncount..)) +
geom_histogram(binwidth=1/50) + facet_grid(.~ label, scales="free")
print(u)

The website says that binwidth defaults to 1/30 of the range. As graph
v shows, range applies to each faceted graph, while the value of
binwidth=1/50 in graph u applies to two both histograms. (Binwidth
also doesn't take vectors; I tried that.)

The question is: How can I change the binwidth to 1/50 of the range
for each faceted graph?

Thanks so much.
Toby

PS: I am new to ggplot; so forgive me if the answer is trivial.

messages.subject: Using annotate() modifies legend symbol
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

This is just a cosmetic issue, but using the annotate() function causes the lower-case letter "a" to appear along with the legend symbol. Here's an example:

t = data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10, type=sample(c("A", "B"), 10, replace=T))
ggplot(t, aes(x=x, y=y, color=type)) + geom_point() + annotate("text", 4, 8, label="Label")

This is with ggplot2 0.8.4 and R 2.10.1.

Thanks,
Jeff

messages.subject: Re: Graph Recommendations
messages.body_plain:
A Simpson's paradox can occur with non significant interaction in the
model but with an interaction term included.  In fact, it most
problematically occurs when there is no interaction but by adding the
interaction term to the model you allow the individual condition lines
to vary freely and the slope reverses.  I'm not sure that this is
strictly a Simpsons paradox based on a quick look at the graph.  Of
course, if I had read the description I might see that that's an
erroneous conclusion in the context... or maybe not.
