>   Wow, the new version of ggplot2 is great, Hadley! Thanks for
>   making the legend parameters more flexible. I have altered the
>   graph (discussed in a previous post) where I wanted one of the
>   2 legends removed.
>
> I have a question for the group (and my apologies in advance if
> this is an inappropriate question for this group): Attached is
> the graph I have been working on and I am very interested in any
> feedback on it. I am really interested in expert opinion about
> how well the graph conveys important information and any
> aesthetic recommendations. Thank you, AC.
>
> Description of graph:
>
> Background.  Previous meta-analyses have concluded that grief
> counseling is effective only for patients experiencing
> complicated grief—i.e., extreme or chronic grief reactions that
> do not abate as normally expected over time.  In this analysis we
> demonstrate that the larger effect sizes for chronic grievers as
> compared with normal grievers are an artifact of differences in
> the length of treatment (number of sessions).  Poor outcomes for
> a third group, so-called at-risk grievers, do appear to be
> significantly lower than those for normal and chronic grievers.
>
> Findings of univariate moderator analyses.  As was the case in
> previous reviews, we found a significant difference in effect

> size (D[+]) by treatment population, where superior outcomes were

> seen in studies involving chronic grievers.  In Figure 1 (below),
> the inset boxplot on the right illustrates this pattern of means,
> with the mean effect size (represented by a ‘+’ symbol) for the
> chronic group hovering at around 1.0, that for the normal group
> closer to 0.5, and even lower mean effects for the at-risk
> group.  (It also shows that the mean for the chronic group is
> quite a bit higher than the median, indicating that the large
> effect size for this group is strongly influenced by three
> studies reporting abnormally large effect sizes.)
>
> Confounds among moderators.  However, the inset boxplot on the
> left in Figure 1 shows that client type (normal, at-risk, or
> chronic) was confounded with another significant moderator
> variable:  number of sessions, or treatment dosage.  In fact, the
> pattern of means for number of sessions mimics quite closely the
> pattern of means for effect size in the other inset boxplot,
> suggesting that the superior effect sizes for the chronic group
> might simply reflect the greater treatment dosage received by
> this group.
>
> The main graph in Figure 1 illustrates how this confounding
> operates.  Effect size is plotted on the y axis as a function of
> number of sessions on the x axis.  Type of grief is represented
> by the shape of the point, with circles, triangles, and squares
> representing normal, at-risk, and chronic grievers,
> respectively.  The size of the point reflects the weight of the
> study in the meta-analysis (mostly a function of sample size,
> with larger points corresponding to studies with larger Ns, which
> therefore provide a more precise estimate of the population
> effect size).
>
> Note the upward trend on this graph, reflecting the importance of
> number of sessions as a predictor of effect size.  As expected,
> studies with longer treatment durations tend to show greater
> effectiveness.  Note too that interventions tended to be longer
> in studies involving chronic grievers, with no study involving an
> intervention with fewer than 12 sessions, whereas many of the
> effect sizes for normal and at-risk grievers were derived from
> studies of interventions involving 10 or fewer sessions.
>
> This figure shows that the straightforward interpretation of the
> differences in risk group means (inset boxplot on the right) may
> be misleading.  The superior effect size for chronic grievers may
> reflect the longer treatments in studies involving this
> population, rather than a greater responsiveness to treatment in
> this group.  To draw clear conclusions about this, it is
> necessary to study dosage and risk group simultaneously as
> predictors of effect size.  As we demonstrate subseauently in our
> multivariate moderator analyses, the apparent difference in
> effectiveness between normal and chronic grievers disappears
> completely when treatment duration is controlled, leading to very
> different conclusions about the importance of risk group, and
> very different implications about who can and cannot benefit from
> grief counseling.

messages.subject: Re: Separate binwidths for faceted histogram
messages.body_plain:
Hi Toby,

Currently, all panels in a layer have to have the same parameters
(mainly because I can't see any nice way of specifying varying
parameters).  You should be able to work around the problem by using
separate layers:

ggplot(dat=dat, aes(x=val, y=..ncount..)) +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(data, label == "a"), binwidth=1/50) +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(data, label == "b"), binwidth=1/10) +

  facet_grid(.~ label, scales="free")

However I'm not on a computer with R at the moment, so I can't double
check that this actually works.

Hadley

> Now I want to highlight the area of above plot starting from May-2008

> do that?

Once you have the coordinate converted to date, you can either:
- select the part of your data that you want to highlight and replot
it with a different colour, e.g.
last_plot() + geom_path(aes(x=dat1, y=whatever),
data=dat[dat$dat1>"2008-05-01" & dat$dat1<"2009-06-30",],
colour="red")
- use annonate() to draw coloured a rectangle above this region of the
graph (see ?annotate)

JiHO
---

2009/12/20 Kim Jung Hwa <kimhwam...@gmail.com>:
> I'm stuck with a legend issue on the following code, if you can help:
>
> "legend box" is currently overlaying with plot's border, I created a
> rectangle around it. Is it possible to move legend box to right so that it
> does not intersect with plot OR is it possible to move it in the plotting
> area (top, right, left, etc...).

As far as I know, the current situation is that opts(legend.position)
supports either "right" (the default), or a custom position inside the
plot with normalised coordinates,

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl), mpg)) +
 geom_boxplot(aes(fill = factor(am)))

p + opts(legend.position = c(0.8, 0.8))

The small overlap with the plot area for position="right" seems to
occur only for half a line width. A quick and dirty workaround would
be to shift the frame by this amount,

theme_rect2 <-
function (fill = NA, colour = "black", size = 0.5, linetype = 1)
{
   structure(function(x = 0.5, y = 0.5, width = 1, height = 1,
       ...) {
             rectGrob(unit(x, "npc") + 0.5*unit(size *ggplot2:::.pt, "pt"), y,
                      width, height, ..., gp = gpar(lwd = size *
           ggplot2:::.pt, col = colour, fill = fill, lty = linetype))

   }, class = "theme", type = "box", call = match.call())
}

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl), mpg)) +
 geom_boxplot(aes(fill = factor(am))) +
 opts(legend.background = theme_rect2())

p

HTH,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ista -

You can do the work of a stat manually with a little work :

df <- data.frame(
  x = rnorm(20),

  y = rnorm(20),
  g = factor(c(rep("A", 2), rep("B", 17), "C"))
)

s <- sort(c(df$x, pretty(extendrange(df$x), n = 101)))

df2 <- data.frame(
  x = rep(s, 3),
  g = rep(factor(c('A','B','C')), each = length(s))
)
df2 <- merge(df2, df, all.x = TRUE)

df2 <- ddply(df2, .(g),
  function(df){
    df  <- df[order(df$x),]
    mod <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
    df$pred <- predict(mod, df[, 'x', drop = FALSE])
    df
  }
)

df2$pred[df2$g == 'C'] <- NA

ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = x, y = y), data = df) +
  geom_path(aes(x = x, y = pred), data = df2) +
  facet_grid(. ~ g)

Is that what you were looking for?

Cheers
david.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Hadley!

In case anyone else is having trouble with this, the following
workaround does work with version 0.8.5:

data <- data.frame(
  x = rnorm(20),

  y = rnorm(20),
  g = factor(c(rep("A", 2), rep("B", 17), "C")))

data2 <- Data[-which(Data$g == "C"),] # remove facet with single values
data2 <- Data[-which(Data$g == "A"),] # need to remove this also
because lm smooth seems to need at least three values

ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE, data=data2) + # plot the smoother
using the reduced dataset
  facet_grid(. ~ g)

-Ista

messages.subject: coord_equal() messes up axis
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

axis labels etc are off with coord_equal(), it is easy to see from an
example:

graafikuks<-data.frame(x=c(0:5), y=c(5:0))
p<-ggplot(graafikuks, aes(x,y))
p<-p+geom_point()
p<-p+coord_equal()
p

first point should be at (0,5) but appears somewhere (-0,25, 5,25)
instead, other points are off too. Without coord_equal() everything
appears as expected.

This seems to be regression in 0.85, it worked in 0.84 (or in 0.83, at
least my previous graphs looked right).

btw - it seems, that the issues are mostly reported here, not in
github? Would it be better to report them in http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/
instead?

Indrek

Hi Amanda,

The problem seems to be with the automatic tick mark selection.  I've
been working with a grad student on a package for dealing with dates
that will eventually fix this problem and will hopefully make it into
a version of ggplot2 early next year.  In the mean time, you can work
around it by explicitly specifying you want a tick every hour:

qplot(Time, Power.now, data = today) + scale_x_datetime(major = "hour")

Hadley

messages.subject: Setting only one limit in coord_cartesian
messages.subject_clean: Setting only one limit in coord_cartesian
messages.body_plain:
I have some data which is inherently positive, and would like to ensure that all graphs in a facet-grid start with y=0, but scale appropriately on the high end.

For example, suppose I'm comparing the growth of hamburger and hot dog sales from year to year:

fr <-
  data.frame(
             year=rep(1:10,2),                                         # 2 runs of 10
             quant=(c(1:10,1:10*3)+rnorm(20,0,3))^2,     # some variation in dependent var
             type=rep(c('hamburgers','hot dogs'),each=10))     # first 10 and second 10 are separate series

and plot it with:

ggplot(fr,aes(x=year,y=quant)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_grid(type~.,scales="free")

This is fine, except that the geom_smooth overflows into (meaningless) negative values.

So I'd like to do something like

   +  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,NA))    # causes internal error

to ensure that the lower y limit is always at 0 to make the graphs comparable.  I do, however, want to let the upper y limit be free.

How do I do this in ggplot?

              -s

messages.subject: Re: Can density be >10?
messages.body_plain:
This is a common question over at R-help. From the help on hist:

density: values f^(x[i]), as estimated density values. If
all(diff(breaks) == 1), they are the relative frequencies counts/n and
in general satisfy sum[i; f^(x[i]) (b[i+1]-b[i])] = 1, where b[i] =
breaks[i].

So, only if the breaks are of size 1 apart will all density values be
less than or equal to 1. Alternatively, sum(density*bin_width) will
always equal 1, so if you want to plot a histogram such that its scale
matches up with some theoretical probability density function, then
plot density*bin_width.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
I think this is what you want. To get a proportion you need to divide
the count by the total count, i.e. sum(..count..)

dat111 <- rnorm(1000)
p <- ggplot(data.frame(dat111), aes(x=dat111))
p + stat_bin(aes(y=..count../sum(..count..)), binwidth=0.5)

HTH

Gary

messages.subject: Re: How to draw line chart with time format like "00:00:00"
messages.subject_clean: How to draw line chart with time format like "00:00:00"
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Dec 24, 2009 at 09:38, Bochao Liu <l...@cert.org.cn> wrote:
> However the chart does not show the lines? Since I am a newbie, could any
> Guru throw any light on it?

not a guru but I'll try.

class(data$time) should show you that R considers the time column as a
factor or as character, i.e. as discrete values, because it has no way
of knowing that they are times on its own. Since they are discrete
values, ggplot won't join them with a line. So you need to tell R that
this is in fact a continuous time scale. To do that, use as.POSIXct()
with the appropriate format and then use your qplot command. You might
then need to reformat the labels with scale_date() if you don't like
what ggplot does by default (but it usually tries to be clever about
which part of the date to show).

JiHO
---

With regard to git and SVN-style merging, what was the verdict?  (i.e., where should I make any changes for consideration in ''HEAD'' ?)

messages.subject: Looking for documentation on theme_bw() for boxplot
messages.subject_clean: Looking for documentation on theme_bw() for boxplot
messages.body_plain:
I used ggplot2 to prepare boxplots of my data6 or 8 months ago, and have generated good plots using theme_bw() that now need a few tweaks to polish for publication.  When I did them the first time, I was able to use the preliminary version of the ggplot book, but now cannot locate documentation that I need to modify the line weight on the boxplot rectangles.  I did find a suggestion to use current.grobTree()but it fails with Error: could not find function "current.grobTree".

When I use a construction like
p <- ggplot(df2,aes(x=Adhesive, y=FailStress_MPa))+geom_boxplot(size=1.5)
I can control the line weight, but of course theme_bw() applied over top of it changes the line weights.
I have also used the "+ opts(<option>) construction to modify the axis text and title, but can't find any equivalent documentation on the parts of the boxplot itself, except for outliers.

I imagine the documentation exists, can someone point me to it? Or suggest a way to manipulate the weight of the boxplots within the b&w theme?

Thank you
Jane

messages.body_plain:
greetings,

I'm trying to plot a grid. I need the x/y axes to be equal length per
unit. the columns are represented by letters similar to Excel. so
first position from the NW most bucket would be A1. I want to display
values associated with either colors or sized circles that draw the
attention of the viewer to areas in the grid that may have
predominately large or small values. I'm almost there but I can't
figure out how to replace the integers on the x-axis with letters
while retaining coord_equal(ratio=1) as a layer.

code so far:

dframe = data.frame(rows=rep(1:4,each=3),cols=rep(1:3,4),val=rnorm
(12)) # rows/cols/val

td + geom_text() + geom_point(shape=15,alpha=I(1/5),aes(size=20*abs
(dframe$val))) +coord_equal()

so the trick I'm missing is to change 1-4 in the x-axis to A-D.

thanks in advance for any help you can provide. and thank you for a
great graphing package.

-Carlo

messages.subject: Re: coord_equal() or substitute names for numbers
messages.subject_clean: coord_equal() or substitute names for numbers
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I don't know if coord_equal can work with discrete scales. You can set
the labels manually with scale_continuous instead,

dframe = data.frame(rows=rep(1:4,each=3),cols=rep(1:3,4),val=rnorm(12))
# rows/cols/val
td = ggplot(aes(rows,cols,label=as.character(round(val))),data=dframe) +
  geom_point(shape=15,alpha=1/5,aes(size=20*abs(dframe$val))) +
  geom_text() +
  coord_equal()

td + scale_x_continuous(breaks=unique(dframe$rows),
label=LETTERS[unique(dframe$rows)])

HTH,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
baptiste_auguie is correct, and I made a dumb mistake.  I am documenting my error here as a cautionary tale.  In short, I forgot that persistent behavior requires assignment eg
# This works and maintains the box line weight
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl), mpg)) +geom_boxplot(size=1.5)+ theme_bw()
p
p + theme_gray()

#This does not because the changes were not assigned to q
q <- qplot(x=factor(cyl), y=mpg, data=mtcars,geom="boxplot", xlab="Xlabel",ylab="Ylabel")
q
q + geom_boxplot(size=1.5)
q + theme_bw()

Finding my error also taught me how to apply a different box line weight to a qplot, which was one of my original goals.

Thanks.
Jane

messages.subject_clean: Axis Labels for Compound Plots in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,
I am trying to stitch together multiple plots using ggplot2
Consider for instance the following snippet based on an old thread
(http://tinyurl.com/ylehm2t)

library(ggplot2)
vplayout <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row=x, layout.pos.col=y)

draw4 <- function(pdfname, a,b,c,d,w,h) {

    pdf(pdfname,width=w, height=h)
    grid.newpage()
    pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(2,2) ) )

        print(a, vp=vplayout(1,1))
        print(b, vp=vplayout(1,2))
        print(c, vp=vplayout(2,1))
        print(d, vp=vplayout(2,2))

    dev.off()
}

data(diamonds)

set.seed(1234)

randind <- sample(nrow(diamonds),1000,replace=FALSE)
dsmall <- diamonds[randind,]

a <-  qplot(carat, data=dsmall, geom="histogram",binwidth=1)
b <-  qplot(carat, data=dsmall, geom="histogram",binwidth=.1)
c <- qplot(carat, data=dsmall, geom="histogram",binwidth=.01)
d <- qplot(carat, data=dsmall, geom="histogram",binwidth=2)

width <- 7
height <- 7

draw4( "test-4.pdf", a,b,c,d, width, height)

Is there any way to give an overall label along the y and x axis?
E.g.something like a xlab to write some text which applies to the x axis
of all the plots and which should go at the middle bottom of the
compound plot (and something perfectly along these lines for the y axis).
Many thanks

Lorenzo

baptiste

messages.subject: Legend not inheriting the alpha values

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Is it possible to make the legend *not* inherit the alpha values of the
geoms? I frequently plot data on rather large datasets, where I have to
use a low value of alpha to avoid overplotting issues. The actual plot
looks good, but the legend becomes unreadable, as the alpha value make
the colour of a single geom almost transparent.

Here's a simple example:

qplot(x,z,data=diamonds, colour=cut, alpha=I(1/40))+xlim(4,10)+ylim(0,10)

(My preferred way of ggplot2 handling this would be to automatically
*not* inherit the alpha value when *setting* it, only when mapping it.)

--
Karl Ove Hufthammer
